query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles to maintain a single‐phase solid solution (and thus both chemical and structural stability) across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges (473–1923 K) is governed by the balance between the high configurational entropy, the pairwise mixing enthalpies among the constituent metals, and their kinetic diffusion barriers. When the mixing enthalpies are small (or moderately favorable) relative to the entropic stabilization and diffusion is sluggish at the operating temperatures, the disordered solid solution is maintained; however, if strong pairwise enthalpic interactions dominate, local ordering (or clustering and surface segregation) will develop, compromising stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized initially as a homogeneous, disordered solid solution.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA nanoparticles to controlled catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions spanning 473–1923 K (with one set having elements chosen for near‐zero mixing enthalpies and a controlled comparison set modified by the addition of an element (e.g., increased Al content) that alters pairwise mixing enthalpy).
generation.conditions: The prediction holds under atmospheres representative of catalytic environments (reactive gas mixtures) and thermoelectric testing environments (inert or controlled atmospheres) with controlled temperature cycling across 473–1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic ordering, clustering, or surface segregation that develop when local pairwise enthalpic interactions overcome the entropic stabilization, potentially altering the homogeneous solid solution.
generation.mechanism: A delicate balance: high configurational entropy tends to favor a disordered, single-phase state, while significant pairwise mixing enthalpies (either strongly attractive or repulsive) drive ordering or segregation. Kinetic diffusion barriers further delay or suppress these rearrangements. Under the operating conditions, if the enthalpic driving force exceeds the thermal stabilization from entropy and the kinetics allow significant atomic rearrangement, microstructural transitions occur.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles where all constituent metals have near-zero or only modest mixing enthalpies (and hence low driving forces for ordering) will remain as a stable, disordered solid solution over the entire temperature range, retaining their expected catalytic/thermoelectric properties. In contrast, nanoparticles with constituents having stronger pairwise interactions (e.g., via minor compositional tweaks such as higher Al content) will exhibit signs of local ordering, clustering or surface segregation (detectable by shifts in diffraction peak positions, emergence of new diffraction features, or changes in catalytic activity) at certain temperatures.
generation.baseline: The initial homogeneous, equiatomic disordered solid solution state without any noticeable short-range order or element segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic prediction is expected to apply to HEA nanoparticle systems where the intrinsic mixing enthalpies are low to moderate and diffusion kinetics are sluggish. In cases where the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation (due to very high positive or negative mixing enthalpies) is overwhelming, or where external reactive environments drastically enhance diffusion, the hypothesis may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative thresholds for the enthalpic contributions and diffusion kinetics under real catalytic/thermoelectric conditions are not precisely defined, and additional factors (e.g., surface oxidation, support interactions) may influence stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles: (a) a reference set with constituent elements chosen such that their pairwise mixing enthalpies are near zero; (b) a modified set in which one element is adjusted (e.g., increased Al content) to introduce significant mixing enthalpy differences. Subject both sets to cyclic exposure under catalytic (reactive gas atmospheres) and thermoelectric (inert or controlled atmosphere) environments spanning 473–1923 K. Use in situ X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to monitor any changes in crystal structure, the emergence of ordering or phase segregation, and correlate these with changes in catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
measurements: In situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns to detect new phases or ordering transitions
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging for local ordering/clustering
Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for elemental segregation
Catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance measurements before and after cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the reference and the modified nanoparticle sets maintain a homogeneous, disordered single-phase solid solution with no detectable local ordering, clustering, or changes in catalytic/thermoelectric properties (as evidenced by stable XRD patterns, TEM images, and performance metrics) across the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis that the balance of mixing enthalpy, configurational entropy, and diffusion kinetics governs the stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] . Using the methods and approximations for accurate estimates of the formation enthalpy and relative energy of A1 and A2 phases [28] , the first-principles KKR-CPA results in Fig. 2 for Al of 0 < x < 2 mole fractions predict a similar global stability found in the experiment, i.e., A1 for x < 0.5, A1 + A2 for 0.5 ≤ Al ≤1.25, and A2 for Al > 1.25.
